title: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
summary: Follow data from discovery to destruction: classification, retention, encryption layers, tokens and masks, database grants and auditing, DLP, insider risk and NIST SP 800-88 sanitisation, with real cases.
outcomes: Find sensitive data with patterns, checksums, context and exact data match, and explain why precision decides DLP
Classify data by impact (FIPS 199, high-water mark) and turn levels into handling, retention and disposal rules
Choose between disk, TDE, field-level, deterministic and enclave encryption by who can still cause decryption
Use tokens, masks, least-privilege grants and views correctly, avoiding the column-revoke and masking inference traps
Audit database reads and detect stage-and-export theft like the 2024 Snowflake intrusions
Explain where DLP can and cannot act, and run an insider risk programme with HR, legal and privacy
Sanitise media with clear, purge, destroy and cryptographic erase, and run disposal with certificates and reconciliation

lessons.title: Seeing security from the data's side: copies, states and stages

blocks.md:
Most security courses start from a system: a server, a network, an app. This one starts from the **data** and follows it around. The questions change: what is this information, where are all its copies, who can read each copy, how can it leave, and when does it stop existing?

A tiny example. A customer uploads a photo of their passport to verify an account.

1. The photo crosses the internet to your API (**in transit**).
2. It is written to a storage bucket (**at rest**).
3. A support agent opens it in a browser to check it (**in use**).
4. The agent pastes a screenshot into a support ticket: a second copy, in a different system with different access rules.
5. The nightly backup copies the bucket: a third copy.
6. Six months later the account is closed. Which copies get deleted?

One upload became three copies in three systems within a day. Data security is the work of knowing about every one of them and protecting each for as long as it exists.

**The three states.** Data is **at rest** when it sits on storage (disks, buckets, databases, backups), **in transit** (also called *in motion*) when it moves over a network, and **in use** when a program or person has it open in memory or on screen. Microsoft's documentation for DLP (data loss prevention: tools that spot sensitive data and stop it leaving, taught in lesson 10) uses the same three words: its policies cover "data at rest, data in use and data in motion". Each state needs different controls: encryption and access rules for rest, TLS for transit (covered in *How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender*), and for use, the harder problem of what someone with legitimate access does next.

**The stages.** This course follows data through six stages, one or more lessons each: *find* it (inventory and discovery), *label* it (classification), *keep less* of it (minimisation and retention), *protect* it (encryption, tokens, masks, database controls), *watch* it leave (auditing, DLP, insider risk) and *destroy* it (media sanitisation).

blocks.title: One upload, many copies: where the data actually lives

scenes.caption: The customer's photo arrives through the API and lands in one bucket. So far there is one copy at rest, protected by the bucket's access policy.
A support agent views it (data in use) and pastes a screenshot into the ticket system. The ticket copy has the ticket system's access rules, not the bucket's.
The nightly backup and an analytics export add two more copies. Nobody decided to create them for this photo; they are side effects of normal operations.
The account closes and the bucket object is deleted. Three copies remain. Each stage of this course closes one of these gaps: find, label, keep less, protect, watch, destroy.

blocks.md: **Case: Pegasus Airlines, 2022.** Researchers at SafetyDetectives, a security comparison website, found an AWS storage bucket left open to the internet on 28 February 2022 and traced it to the Electronic Flight Bag (EFB) software of Pegasus Airlines, a Turkish low-cost carrier. An EFB is the software crews use for flight reference material. According to [Infosecurity Magazine's report](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/turkish-airline-exposes-flight/), the bucket held almost 23 million files, about 6.5 TB: more than three million files of flight data (charts, insurance documents, pre-flight check issues, crew shifts), over 1.6 million files with crew personal data including photos and signatures, and EFB source code containing plain-text passwords and secret keys. The researchers notified the airline on 1 March and the exposure was fixed about three weeks later. There was no indication anyone malicious found it first.

**Reading Pegasus from the data's side.** Every stage of this course had a gap:

- *Find*: one bucket mixed flight data, personal data and source code. A discovery scan would have reported personal data and credentials in a place where neither belonged.
- *Label*: crew photos and signatures are personal data; passwords and keys are secrets. Either label should have forced a stricter storage rule than "a bucket the EFB team uses".
- *Keep less*: secrets do not belong in source code at all, and old crew records need a deletion date.
- *Protect*: the account-wide public access guardrail (lesson *Storage exposure: public buckets, Block Public Access and SAS tokens* in *Cloud security and IAM*) stops one bucket policy from making data public.
- *Watch*: the owner did not notice; outsiders did. You want your own scans to find it first.

The Microsoft AI research SAS token of 2023, taught in that same Cloud security lesson, is the same story with a different storage service: one over-broad link exposed 38 TB.

blocks.md: Start every data security question from the data: what is it, where are *all* its copies (including tickets, exports and backups), who can read each one, how can it leave, and when will each copy be destroyed.

blocks.question: A team encrypts its production database and restricts access to three engineers. Which copy of the same customer data is most likely to be forgotten?
options: The database's own data files
A CSV export an analyst saved to a shared drive for a one-off report
The database's encryption key in the key management service
The TLS session between the app and the database
blocks.explain: Exports, tickets, screenshots and backups are side-effect copies. They inherit none of the database's controls and usually have no owner or deletion date. The data files are what the team protected; the key and the TLS session are not copies of customer data.

blocks.question: In the Pegasus case, which finding shows the bucket held more than personal data?
options: It contained over 1.6 million crew files
It was open from February 2022
It was fixed three weeks after notification
Its source code contained plain-text passwords and secret keys, which could unlock other systems
blocks.explain: Credentials in a leaked bucket extend the exposure beyond the bucket itself: SafetyDetectives warned the keys could let someone tamper with flight data. Personal data and dates matter, but they do not show the leak reaching other systems.

lessons.title: Finding sensitive data: inventories, patterns, checksums and context

blocks.md:
You cannot protect data you do not know you have. A **data inventory** (also called a data map) is a list of every place sensitive data lives: the system, what kinds of data it holds, who owns it, where it is hosted, who can read it and when it must be deleted. Writing the first version by asking teams is useful, but it is always incomplete, because of the side-effect copies from lesson 1.

So organisations also run **discovery**: tools that open files, objects and database rows and look for sensitive content. Examples: **Amazon Macie**, which AWS describes as discovering sensitive data in S3 "by using machine learning and pattern matching"; **Microsoft Purview**, Microsoft's data security and compliance product family, whose built-in *sensitive information types* (SITs) recognise things like card numbers and national identifiers; and **Google Sensitive Data Protection**. They all work in the same basic way, and the same detectors power the DLP tools in lessons 10 and 11.

**How a detector recognises a card number.** Microsoft documents its credit card SIT precisely, and it shows the four ingredients every good detector uses:

1. **Pattern**: 14 to 19 digits, formatted or not, matching the number formats of the major card brands.
2. **Checksum**: the digits must pass the Luhn test (below).
3. **Context**: supporting evidence within 300 characters, such as a keyword like "cvv2" or "security code", a cardholder-name keyword, or an expiry date.
4. **Confidence**: pattern plus checksum alone gives *low* confidence (level 65); pattern plus checksum plus one piece of context gives *high* confidence (level 85).

Microsoft also notes the type does not flag reserved test numbers that banks use for testing. A detector built this way is cheap to run over millions of files and wrong in predictable ways, which you will see below.

**The Luhn check.** Hans Peter Luhn, working for IBM, filed a patent in January 1954 (granted 1960) for a ["computer for verifying numbers"](https://patents.google.com/patent/US2950048A/en). Its purpose was catching copying mistakes, such as two swapped digits, in long part numbers: a check digit is appended so that a simple sum comes out to a multiple of 10. Card numbers use the same scheme. It is not a security feature; it is a typo detector. For a discovery tool it is a cheap filter: random digit strings mostly fail it.

The rule: starting from the rightmost digit, double every second digit; if doubling gives more than 9, subtract 9; add everything up. The number passes if the total is divisible by 10.

blocks.tex: \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} f_i(d_{n-1-i}) \equiv 0 \pmod{10}, \qquad f_i(d)=\begin{cases} d & i \text{ even} \\ 2d \text{ or } 2d-9 \text{ if } 2d>9 & i \text{ odd}\end{cases}
blocks.caption: Digits are counted from the right (i = 0 is the last digit). Every odd position is doubled, with 9 subtracted from results above 9.

blocks.title: The Luhn check on two 16-digit numbers

scenes.caption: The well-known test card number 4111 1111 1111 1111. Positions counted from the right: the last digit is position 0, so the first digit is position 15.
Every second digit from the right (positions 1, 3, 5 ... 15) is doubled. The leading 4 becomes 8; each 1 in a doubled position becomes 2. Undoubled digits stay as they are.
The sum is 8 + 7 x 2 + 8 x 1 = 30, divisible by 10: the number passes. A detector would now look for context nearby.
Change only the last digit to 2 (a typo). The sum becomes 31, not divisible by 10: the check fails, and a detector drops the match before looking at context.

blocks.prompt: Roughly what fraction of random 16-digit strings pass the Luhn check, and what does that mean for a scanner looking at log files full of long numeric IDs?
blocks.reveal: About **1 in 10**. For any 15 leading digits there is exactly one last digit that makes the sum divisible by 10. So a log with a million random 16-digit trace IDs contains around 100,000 that pass Luhn. That is why the third sample above matched: `trace_id=7305918264095522` passes the checksum but is not a card. The checksum removes 90% of noise; context and confidence levels have to handle the rest.

blocks.md: A match is evidence, not proof. Pattern plus checksum gives low confidence; only context (keywords, expiry dates, nearby names) raises it. Tune discovery and DLP rules to act on high confidence and review the low-confidence bucket, rather than blocking on every 16-digit number.

**Defender view.** Run discovery on a schedule over every data store you know about, and over the places where copies appear: file shares, ticket attachments, chat exports, storage buckets, data warehouses. Feed the results into the inventory, so a bucket that "only holds logs" but contains card numbers becomes a finding with an owner. Treat a discovery hit in an unexpected place as an incident to investigate: how did it get there, and who could read it?

blocks.question: A Purview-style rule finds a Luhn-valid 16-digit number with no keywords or dates within 300 characters. What should the confidence be?
options: Low: pattern and checksum without supporting context
High: the checksum proves it is a card
None: without a keyword it is discarded
High, because test numbers are excluded
blocks.explain: In Microsoft's documented definition, pattern plus checksum alone is the low-confidence pattern (65). High confidence (85) needs one of the context conditions. About 1 in 10 random numbers pass Luhn, so the checksum alone proves little.

blocks.question: Why is the Luhn check useful in a discovery tool even though it offers no security?
options: It can only be computed by the card issuer
It encrypts the number
It cheaply discards about 90% of random digit strings before more expensive context checks
It identifies the card's owner
blocks.explain: Luhn was designed to catch transcription errors. Any 15 digits have exactly one valid check digit, so random strings pass only about 10% of the time: a cheap filter that cuts noise before the detector looks for keywords and dates.

lessons.title: Classification: levels, impact and the high-water mark

blocks.md:
Discovery tells you what data exists. **Classification** decides how much protection each kind deserves, so that the strongest (and most expensive, most annoying) controls go where the damage would be worst. A **classification scheme** is a short list of levels with a rule for assigning them and a handling rule for each.

Tiny example: a company with three kinds of data. Its marketing brochure can be public. Its org chart can leak without real harm but should stay internal. Its payroll file would hurt people if it leaked. Treating all three the same means either over-protecting the brochure or under-protecting payroll.

**Government classification.** US national security information is classified under Executive Order 13526 (2009) at three levels, defined by the damage unauthorised disclosure "reasonably could be expected to cause" to national security:

- **Top Secret**: "exceptionally grave damage"
- **Secret**: "serious damage"
- **Confidential**: "damage"

Each must be damage that the classifying official "is able to identify or describe". The order also builds in an end date: information is normally marked for declassification 10 years from the original decision, or up to 25 years when its sensitivity requires.

**Business classification.** Companies write their own schemes. A common shape is four levels, for example *Public*, *Internal*, *Confidential* and *Restricted*, but names and counts vary; what matters is that each level has a damage-based definition and a concrete handling rule.

**Rating impact on three axes: FIPS 199.** NIST's FIPS 199 (Federal Information Processing Standard 199, 2004), used by US federal agencies, rates each *information type* separately for confidentiality, integrity and availability (the CIA triad from *Security from zero*), each as **LOW** (a "limited adverse effect"), **MODERATE** ("serious") or **HIGH** ("severe or catastrophic"). It writes the result as a security category:

`SC investigative information = {(confidentiality, HIGH), (integrity, MODERATE), (availability, MODERATE)}`

FIPS 199's own example for public information has confidentiality *NOT APPLICABLE*: nothing is lost if it is disclosed, but tampering still matters. For a whole **system**, FIPS 199 takes the **high-water mark**: the highest value for each objective among all the information types the system holds. One sensitive dataset raises the whole system.

blocks.title: FIPS 199 high-water mark for an HR system

scenes.caption: Three information types in one HR system, rated separately (0 = not applicable, 1 = LOW, 2 = MODERATE, 3 = HIGH). Simplified example; ratings are illustrative.
Confidentiality: the highest value among the types is HIGH, from background checks. The whole system's confidentiality becomes HIGH.
Integrity is HIGH because of payroll (a tampered salary is serious harm), availability MODERATE. The system row is the column-wise maximum.
Move background checks to their own system (their row now shows zeros) and this system's confidentiality drops to MODERATE. Separating data shrinks the area that needs the strictest controls.

blocks.caption: Python 3, run as shown. Output: `SC HR system = {(confidentiality, HIGH), (integrity, HIGH), (availability, MODERATE)}`. For systems FIPS 199 allows only LOW, MODERATE or HIGH.

blocks.md:
**Who decides, and how the label travels.** The **data owner**, the business person accountable for a dataset, decides its classification; the teams that run the systems apply the handling rules. A classification is only useful if it travels with the data. Tools do this with **labels**: Microsoft Purview *sensitivity labels*, for example, are attached to documents and emails, can apply encryption and visible markings (headers, footers, watermarks), and can restrict what specified people may do with the content. DLP rules (lessons 10 and 11) can then key on the label rather than re-detecting the content every time.

**A handling matrix** turns levels into rules engineers can follow. For each level, state: where it may be stored, whether encryption at the field level is required, who may approve access, whether it may leave the company and by which channel, how long it is kept, and how media holding it is sanitised. NIST SP 800-88 explicitly ties sanitisation choices to the FIPS 199 confidentiality level (lesson 13).

Classify by the damage of disclosure (and of tampering or loss), not by how the data looks. Rate each information type, take the high-water mark for systems, and attach the result as a label that tools can read.

blocks.question: A system stores public product photos (confidentiality not applicable, integrity LOW, availability LOW) and customer support chats (confidentiality MODERATE, integrity LOW, availability LOW). What is its FIPS 199 confidentiality?
options: NOT APPLICABLE, because most of its data is public
LOW, the average
MODERATE, the highest value among its information types
HIGH, because it is customer-facing
blocks.explain: FIPS 199 uses the high-water mark: the system's value for each objective is the highest among its information types. Volume and averages do not matter; the support chats set confidentiality to MODERATE.

blocks.question: Under Executive Order 13526, what distinguishes Secret from Confidential?
options: The expected damage from disclosure: serious damage for Secret, damage for Confidential
Secret covers foreign information only
Who wrote the document
Secret information can never be declassified
blocks.explain: The three levels are defined by the damage unauthorised disclosure could reasonably be expected to cause to national security: exceptionally grave (Top Secret), serious (Secret), damage (Confidential). Declassification dates apply to all levels.

lessons.title: Keep less: minimisation, retention schedules and legal holds

blocks.md:
The cheapest data to protect is data you never collected or already deleted. It cannot leak, be stolen, be subpoenaed or need a breach notice. This is a security control, not just a privacy courtesy.

Tiny example: an app verifies age by asking users to upload a photo ID. Once a person has been verified, the app needs one bit (*verified: yes, on this date*). Keeping the ID photo afterwards adds nothing to the product and creates a store of identity documents that attackers would love.

**The law says it too.** The EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, introduced in *Risk, governance and compliance for engineers*) lists principles in Article 5. Two of them are this lesson:

- **Data minimisation** (Article 5(1)(c)): personal data must be "adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed".
- **Storage limitation** (Article 5(1)(e)): kept "in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary" for those purposes (with exceptions for archiving and research under safeguards).

Article 25, data protection by design and by default, asks controllers to build such measures, pseudonymisation among them, into processing from the start.

**Case: Tea, July 2025.** Tea is a dating-safety app on which women run background checks on men and share warnings about men they have dated. In July 2025 it confirmed "unauthorised access" to 72,000 images submitted by users, [reported by BBC News](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c7vl57n74pqo). Some were images of women holding photo identification for verification, which Tea's own privacy policy said were "deleted immediately" after authentication. Tea said the breach affected members who signed up before February 2024, and later admitted that a further 59,000 images of posts, comments and direct messages had been accessed.

From the data's side: the purpose (verification) was finished, the policy promised deletion, and the copies still existed. A written retention rule only protects people if a job actually enforces it, in every place the data was copied.

**A retention schedule** says, for each kind of record: how long to keep it, what event starts the clock (creation, verification, account closure, end of contract), why (a law, a contract, a business need) and what happens at the end (delete, anonymise, archive). Engineers turn each line into a job that runs every day.

**Legal holds.** When litigation or an investigation is expected, lawyers place a hold on the relevant records, and deletion must stop for them until the hold is released. Tools encode this priority: in Microsoft Purview, the first principle of retention is that "retention wins over deletion", and holds for legal cases (eDiscovery holds; eDiscovery means finding and preserving electronic records for legal proceedings) also block deletion. Purview even has a separate *priority cleanup* feature that can override such holds, for cases like data that spilled where it should never have been.

blocks.code:
import sqlite3
from datetime import date, timedelta

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE id_photos (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, user_id INT,
                        verified_on TEXT, legal_hold INT DEFAULT 0);
INSERT INTO id_photos (user_id, verified_on, legal_hold) VALUES
  (11, '2023-11-02', 0), (12, '2024-01-20', 1),
  (13, '2026-11-20', 0), (14, '2026-11-21', 0);
""")

RETAIN = timedelta(days=30)             # schedule: delete 30 days after verification
today = date(2026, 11, 22)
cutoff = (today - RETAIN).isoformat()

held = db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM id_photos WHERE verified_on < ? AND legal_hold = 1",
                  (cutoff,)).fetchone()[0]
cur = db.execute("DELETE FROM id_photos WHERE verified_on < ? AND legal_hold = 0", (cutoff,))
print("cutoff:", cutoff)
print("deleted:", cur.rowcount, "| kept by legal hold:", held)
print("left:", db.execute("SELECT user_id, verified_on FROM id_photos").fetchall())
