blocks.title: One ID photo under a 30-day retention rule

scenes.caption: Day 0: the user verifies and the photo is stored. The schedule says: delete 30 days after verification. Scale is in days.
Day 1: the nightly backup copies the photo. This copy is kept 35 days (to day 36); every later nightly backup also holds the photo for 35 days, so copies can outlive the primary by up to five weeks.

Day 30: the job deletes the primary. The day-1 backup expires on day 36, but every nightly backup up to day 29 also holds the photo, so the last copy lives to day 64. Exposure lasts as long as the longest copy.
Same photo, but a legal hold arrives on day 20. The job skips it: retention wins over deletion until the hold is released, and the lawyers own that decision.
The broken version (the Tea pattern): the policy says delete, but no job runs. The photo stays indefinitely, in every copy.

blocks.md: Deleting the primary copy is not deletion. Exports, tickets, caches, logs and backups each need their own retention, and backups usually expire last. Lesson 13 shows a way to make old backups unreadable all at once: encrypt them and destroy the key.
Collect only what the purpose needs, give every record type a retention period and a trigger, enforce it with a job (not a policy document), and make legal holds the only thing that stops the job.

blocks.question: An app keeps ID photos 'until verification is complete', but the deletion job only runs on the main bucket. Which copy most extends the exposure window?
options: The main bucket
The user's phone
The TLS session used for upload
The backup set with its own longer retention, plus any copies in tickets or exports
blocks.explain: Exposure lasts as long as the longest-lived copy. Backups and side-effect copies have their own retention, and nobody deletes them when the main record goes. The upload session is gone in seconds; the phone is outside the company's control and is not a copy the company holds.

blocks.question: A deletion job meets a record that is under a legal hold and past its retention date. What should it do?
options: Delete it, because retention dates are mandatory
Skip it and log that it was skipped because of the hold
Anonymise it instead
Ask the user
blocks.explain: Holds override deletion until legal releases them (Purview's 'retention wins over deletion'). Deleting held records can be a serious legal problem; changing them by anonymising is also a change. The job should skip and record why, so the record is deleted once the hold ends.

lessons.title: Encryption at rest, layer by layer: disk, database, field

blocks.md:
"Is it encrypted?" is the wrong question. The useful one is: **who can cause it to be decrypted?** Every encryption-at-rest layer protects against people who hold the storage but not the key path. Anyone who can make the system decrypt for them, because the system does it automatically for an authorised caller, is not stopped at all.

You know the building blocks already: AES-GCM and associated data from *Cryptography for engineers*, and KMS envelope encryption and SSE-KMS from the lesson *Secrets and keys: KMS, envelope encryption and secret stores* in *Cloud security and IAM*. This lesson is about **where** in the stack you apply them.

**The layers, from the bottom up.**

- **Full disk encryption (FDE)**: NIST SP 800-111 (Guide to Storage Encryption Technologies for End User Devices) describes it as encrypting all the data on a disk, usually with **pre-boot authentication**: the user proves who they are before the operating system loads. Once the machine is running and unlocked, every program sees plaintext. Volume, virtual disk and file/folder encryption are narrower variants of the same idea.
- **Storage service encryption**: a cloud provider encrypting objects or volumes (SSE-KMS). Same property: an authorised API call gets plaintext.

Higher up, inside the database and the application:

- **Database encryption**: **TDE** (transparent data encryption) in SQL Server encrypts the data and log files at page level: pages are encrypted before they are written to disk and decrypted when read into memory. It is "transparent" because, in Microsoft's words, it works "without changing existing applications". Microsoft's stated threat: someone who steals drives or backup tapes and restores the database elsewhere. TDE does not encrypt traffic, and every query by a permitted user returns plaintext.
- **Application-level (field-level) encryption**: the application encrypts individual values, such as a national ID number (in the US, the Social Security number or SSN), before sending them to the database. The database, its administrators and its backups hold only ciphertext; only code with access to the key sees plaintext.

blocks.title: Which layer stops which threat (1 = stops it)

scenes.caption: Simplified model of a database server. Rows are threats, columns are layers. Pulling the physical disk is stopped by every layer, which is why 'encrypted at rest' sounds so reassuring.
A backup file copied to another server: FDE protected only the original disk, so it does nothing. TDE stops it if the certificate is not copied with it. Field-level values stay ciphertext.
A database administrator, or anyone with SELECT, reads the table. FDE and TDE decrypt automatically for them. Only field-level encryption, with keys outside the database, keeps the values unreadable.

An attacker logs in with the application's own stolen credentials. Every layer decrypts for the app, so none helps. This was the OPM situation: identity and detection controls matter here, not encryption.

blocks.md: **Case: OPM, 2015.** The US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) lost sensitive personnel and background-investigation data on millions of US government employees and contractors. At a June 2015 congressional hearing, OPM's director, Katherine Archuleta, was asked why the data had not been encrypted and said encryption was "not feasible to implement on networks that are too old"; the chief information officer (CIO), Donna Seymour, said some systems were over 20 years old and written in COBOL, a decades-old business programming language. But Andy Ozment, then Assistant Secretary for Cybersecurity at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), testified that encryption would "not have helped in this case", because the attackers had valid user credentials and there was no multi-factor authentication, [as Ars Technica reported](https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2015/06/encryption-would-not-have-helped-at-opm-says-dhs-official/). That is the bottom row of the matrix.

**Field-level encryption done right.** Encrypt each sensitive value with an AEAD cipher (AES-GCM) under a data key from your KMS, and pass **associated data** that names the cell: table, row id and column. The associated data is not secret and not stored in the ciphertext, but decryption fails if it differs. That stops an insider with write access from copying an encrypted value from one row into another (for example, moving someone else's bank account number into their own record) without being detected.

blocks.code:
import os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidTag

key = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)   # in production: a data key from KMS
aead = AESGCM(key)

def seal(row_id: int, column: str, value: str) -> bytes:
    nonce = os.urandom(12)
    aad = f"customers:{row_id}:{column}".encode()     # binds ciphertext to its cell
    return nonce + aead.encrypt(nonce, value.encode(), aad)

def open_(row_id: int, column: str, blob: bytes) -> str:
    aad = f"customers:{row_id}:{column}".encode()
    return aead.decrypt(blob[:12], blob[12:], aad).decode()

ana = seal(1, "ssn", "123-45-6789")
kim = seal(2, "ssn", "987-65-4321")
print("stored bytes:", len(ana))   # 12 nonce + 11 ciphertext + 16 tag
print("row 1 reads:", open_(1, "ssn", ana))

# An insider with write access copies Ana's ciphertext into Kim's row
try:
    print("row 2 reads:", open_(2, "ssn", ana))
except InvalidTag:
    print("row 2 reads: InvalidTag (ciphertext was moved between rows)")
blocks.caption: Python 3 with the `cryptography` package, run as shown. Output: `stored bytes: 39`, `row 1 reads: 123-45-6789`, `row 2 reads: InvalidTag (ciphertext was moved between rows)`.

blocks.md:
**The costs of field-level encryption.** The database can no longer index, sort, search or join on the plaintext; every consumer needs key access and a library; key rotation means re-encrypting values. Lesson 6 covers the techniques that give some of that back. Use it for the few fields where the bottom-two-rows threats are real: national IDs, bank details, health conditions, secrets.

**Defender view.** Keys belong in a KMS or an HSM (hardware security module: a tamper-resistant device that holds keys and uses them without letting them out), never in the same database or repository as the data. Every decrypt is a logged API call, so a spike in `Decrypt` calls by one role is a detection signal, and denying `Decrypt` to analytics roles is a real control.

"Encrypted at rest" in a compliance checklist usually means disk, storage or TDE encryption. It answers stolen hardware and copied backups. It does nothing against SQL access, application bugs or stolen credentials, which is how most data is actually taken.

blocks.question: Which control keeps a database administrator from reading customers' national ID numbers?
options: Field-level encryption in the application, with keys in a KMS the DBA cannot use
Full disk encryption on the database server
TDE with the certificate in the master database
TLS between the application and the database
blocks.explain: FDE and TDE decrypt automatically for anyone the database lets in, including administrators. TLS protects data in transit only. Field-level encryption keeps values as ciphertext inside the database, so only code with key access sees them.

blocks.question: Why bind the row id and column name as associated data when encrypting a field?
options: It makes the ciphertext shorter
It hides the row id
Decryption fails if an encrypted value is moved to another row or column, so swaps are detected
It removes the need for a nonce
blocks.explain: Associated data is authenticated but not encrypted. Decrypting with different associated data raises InvalidTag, as the demo shows. It does not hide or shorten anything, and AES-GCM still needs a unique nonce per encryption.

lessons.title: Searching encrypted data: deterministic encryption and enclaves

blocks.md:
Field-level encryption with a random nonce means the same national ID encrypts to different bytes every time. Secure, but the database cannot answer `WHERE ssn = '123-45-6789'`, cannot join two tables on it, cannot group by it. Products restore some of these abilities, and each one gives back a little information. This lesson shows exactly what.

Tiny example: a `region` column with three possible values. If equal plaintexts always produce equal ciphertexts, anyone who can see the column can count how many rows share each ciphertext, even without the key.

**Always Encrypted** (Microsoft SQL Server and Azure SQL) is a concrete design. An Always Encrypted-enabled client driver encrypts sensitive columns before sending them and decrypts results, rewriting queries automatically. Two keys: a **column encryption key** encrypts the data in a column; a **column master key** encrypts the column encryption keys and is kept outside the database, in Azure Key Vault, the Windows certificate store or a hardware security module. Microsoft's documentation states that the database engine "doesn't store or use any keys in plaintext".

It offers two kinds of encryption:

- **Deterministic**: the same plaintext always gives the same ciphertext. That allows point lookups, equality joins, grouping and indexing. Microsoft's warning: unauthorised users "might guess information about encrypted values by examining patterns in the encrypted column, especially if there's a small set of possible encrypted values, such as True/False, or North/South/East/West region".
- **Randomized**: identical inputs give different outputs; no searching, grouping, indexing or joining on the column without enclaves.

blocks.code:
import hmac, hashlib, os
from collections import Counter

key = os.urandom(32)

def det_token(value: str) -> str:            # deterministic: same in, same out
    return hmac.new(key, value.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()[:8]

regions = ["North"] * 6 + ["South"] * 3 + ["East"] * 1
column = [det_token(r) for r in regions]      # what the database stores

counts = Counter(column).most_common()
print("distinct tokens:", len(counts))
print("token counts:   ", [n for _, n in counts])
# Public knowledge: most customers live in the North, fewest in the East.
guess = dict(zip([t for t, _ in counts], ["North", "South", "East"]))
right = sum(guess[t] == r for t, r in zip(column, regions))
print("rows decoded by frequency alone:", right, "of", len(regions))
blocks.caption: Python 3, run as shown. Output: `distinct tokens: 3`, `token counts: [6, 3, 1]`, `rows decoded by frequency alone: 10 of 10`. HMAC stands in for any deterministic scheme: the leak comes from determinism, not from the algorithm.

blocks.title: Frequency analysis of a deterministically encrypted column

scenes.caption: What an attacker with read access sees: three distinct ciphertexts and how many rows carry each. No key is involved.
What the attacker already knows from public statistics: most customers are in the North, fewer in the South, fewest in the East (shown as rows out of 10).
Match the two rankings: A is North, B is South, C is East. All 10 rows are decoded. Randomized encryption shows ten different ciphertexts and defeats this.

blocks.md: **Enclaves: computing inside protected hardware.** The Confidential Computing Consortium, an industry group, defines **confidential computing** as "the protection of data in use using hardware-based, attested Trusted Execution Environments". A **trusted execution environment** (TEE) is an environment that provides data confidentiality, data integrity and code integrity, so that, in the Consortium's words, unauthorised entities, including "the host operating system and hypervisor, system administrators, service providers, and the infrastructure owner", cannot read or change what happens inside. **Attestation** is how a client checks, before trusting it, that the enclave is genuine and runs the expected code.

Always Encrypted *with secure enclaves* applies this to the database. The engine processes encrypted data inside a **secure enclave**, a protected memory region: Intel SGX (Software Guard Extensions), a CPU feature, or Windows virtualization-based security (VBS), which is software built on the Windows hypervisor and needs no special hardware. SQL Server supports only VBS enclaves, and Microsoft ends support for SGX enclaves in Azure SQL on 31 October 2027, which allows pattern matching, comparisons, sorting and in-place encryption on randomized columns. Its attestation verifies that the enclave is genuine and runs the Microsoft-signed enclave library; Microsoft calls it a defence-in-depth check that can help detect administrators tampering with the enclave or its environment.

blocks.title: Always Encrypted: where the keys and the plaintext live

scenes.caption: The client driver holds access to the column master key in a key store. It encrypts the SSN before the query leaves the application.
The database stores and returns only ciphertext. Administrators and backups see ciphertext. Equality lookups work only on deterministic columns.
With a secure enclave, the driver checks the enclave through an attestation service and then lets it use the keys, so the server can compare and sort randomized values inside the enclave.

What you now trust: the driver, the key store, the enclave and its attestation. The DBA is outside that set. The host OS is outside it only with Intel SGX; VBS enclaves give no protection against privileged accounts on the host.

blocks.md:
**Other ways to compute on protected data.** The Consortium's white paper compares hardware TEEs with **homomorphic encryption** (mathematics that lets a server compute on ciphertext without ever decrypting it) and with secure elements such as a TPM (Trusted Platform Module, a security chip on the computer), which protect keys only. The paper's comparison table credits homomorphic encryption with data confidentiality but not code integrity: the server computes on ciphertext, but nothing proves it ran the computation you asked for.

**Choosing.** Randomized encryption for fields nobody searches; deterministic only for high-cardinality identifiers you must look up by equality (account numbers, not booleans or regions); enclaves when you need range queries or sorting on protected columns and can accept trusting the hardware vendor and attestation chain.

Every query ability you add to encrypted data leaks something: deterministic encryption leaks equality and frequency, so never use it on low-cardinality columns. Enclaves add order: randomized columns that support range queries leak the order of values to anyone who can scan the index. They move trust from the administrator to the enclave and its attestation, and only SGX keeps out the host OS.

blocks.question: A team wants to encrypt an `is_vip` boolean column but still filter on it. Why is deterministic encryption a poor choice?
options: Deterministic encryption cannot encrypt booleans
It is slower than randomized encryption
It requires a secure enclave
With only two values, each ciphertext appears in many rows, and counting them (plus any known fact about one row) reveals every row's value
blocks.explain: Deterministic encryption maps each plaintext to one ciphertext. With two possible values, there are two ciphertexts; knowing the VIP rate or one VIP customer decodes all rows. Microsoft's documentation warns about exactly this for True/False columns.

blocks.question: What does attestation give a client of a secure enclave?
options: Encryption of data in transit
Evidence, checked before any keys are shared, that the enclave is genuine and runs the expected code
A backup of the column master key
A guarantee that no side channel exists
blocks.explain: Attestation is how the client decides the enclave is genuine and runs the expected code. It is not transport encryption or key backup, and it does not prove the hardware is free of side-channel weaknesses.

lessons.title: Tokens and masks: taking real values out of systems

blocks.md:
The strongest protection for a value in a system is for the system not to have it. **Tokenisation** replaces a sensitive value with a stand-in, a **token**, that is useless on its own; the real value lives in one tightly controlled place. **Masking** shows a partly hidden version (`************1111`) to people and systems that do not need the whole value.

Tiny example: an online shop needs to show customers "Visa ending 1111", issue refunds and spot repeat buyers. None of that needs the full card number in the orders database. Only the payment step does.

**Vault tokenisation.** A token service generates a **random** token for each value and stores the mapping. Because the token is random, there is no mathematics linking it to the value: stealing the orders table gives tokens, and only the vault can map back (**detokenise**). The vault becomes the one system that needs the strongest controls, logging and audits, and everything that holds only tokens can shrink its compliance scope. You saw the payment version, card entry through the payment provider so that you store only tokens, in the PCI DSS lesson of *Risk, governance and compliance for engineers*.

blocks.code:
import secrets

class TokenVault:
    """Toy vault: the only place the real numbers live."""
    def __init__(self):
        self._by_token, self._by_value = {}, {}

    def tokenize(self, pan: str) -> str:
        if pan in self._by_value:                  # same card, same token
            return self._by_value[pan]
        token = "tok_" + secrets.token_hex(8)      # random: no maths links it to pan
        self._by_token[token], self._by_value[pan] = pan, token
        return token

    def detokenize(self, token: str, caller: str) -> str:
        if caller != "refund-service":            # policy check, and log it
            raise PermissionError(f"{caller} may not detokenize")
        return self._by_token[token]

vault = TokenVault()
t1 = vault.tokenize("4111111111111111")
t2 = vault.tokenize("4111111111111111")
print("same token for same card:", t1 == t2, "| length:", len(t1))
print("orders table stores:", t1[:4] + "...")
print("refund service sees last 4:", vault.detokenize(t1, "refund-service")[-4:])
try:
    vault.detokenize(t1, "analytics-job")
except PermissionError as e:
    print("PermissionError:", e)
blocks.caption: Python 3, run as shown. Output: `same token for same card: True | length: 20`, `orders table stores: tok_...`, `refund service sees last 4: 1111`, `PermissionError: analytics-job may not detokenize`. A toy: a real vault is a hardened service with its own database, HSM-backed keys and audit log.

blocks.title: Who may turn a token back into a card number

scenes.caption: Checkout sends the card number to the vault once. The vault returns a random token.
The orders database stores only the token. A breach of this database exposes tokens, which are meaningless outside the vault.
An analytics job reads orders and asks the vault to detokenise. Policy says no; the denial is logged and is itself a signal worth reviewing.

The refund service is allowed: it detokenises, and the vault logs who asked, when and why. Analytics still works on tokens, because the same card always gets the same token (which, like deterministic encryption, reveals equal values and their counts).

blocks.md:
**Vaultless (cryptographic) tokens.** Instead of a lookup table, a key turns the value into the token. Google's Sensitive Data Protection documents three methods, all keyed:

- **Deterministic encryption with AES-SIV** (SIV: synthetic initialization vector, a mode from [RFC 5297](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5297) designed to be deterministic safely): reversible with the key, keeps referential integrity, does not preserve format.
- **Format-preserving encryption, FPE-FFX** (FFX is a Feistel-based FPE design, where a Feistel network splits the input into two halves and mixes them over several keyed rounds; NIST says the X marks its flexible parameter sets, and FF1 is one instance of it): output has the same length and alphabet as the input, so a 16-digit number stays 16 digits and fits existing columns and validators. Reversible with the key.
- **HMAC-SHA-256**: one-way; equal inputs give equal outputs for joins and counts, but there is no way back.

FPE has a cautionary history. NIST approved two methods, FF1 and FF3, in SP 800-38G (2016). After attacks on small input domains, the draft revision makes a minimum domain of one million values a requirement; after a further weakness in FF3's tweak schedule, the second draft (February 2025) drops FF3 entirely. Use FF1 from a maintained library, never on small domains such as a 4-digit PIN.

**Pseudonymised is still personal.** GDPR defines **pseudonymisation** (Article 4(5)) as processing so that data "can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information", provided that information is kept separately and protected. Recital 26 adds that pseudonymised data which could be attributed to a person using that additional information "should be considered to be information on an identifiable natural person". Tokens reduce risk and scope; they do not take data outside data protection law.

**Masking.** *Static* masking writes a permanently altered copy, for example a production database copied into a test environment with names replaced and card numbers reduced to the last four digits. *Dynamic* masking hides values at query time while the stored data stays real.

blocks.code:
import re

def mask_email(e: str) -> str:
    user, _, domain = e.partition("@")
    return user[0] + "***@" + domain

def mask_pan(p: str) -> str:
    digits = re.sub(r"\D", "", p)
    return "*" * (len(digits) - 4) + digits[-4:]

def mask_phone(ph: str) -> str:
    return re.sub(r"\d(?=(?:\D*\d){4})", "X", ph)   # keep last 4 digits

print(mask_email("ana.ruiz@example.com"))
print(mask_pan("4111 1111 1111 1111"))
print(mask_phone("555.123.1234"))
blocks.caption: Python 3, run as shown. Output: `a***@example.com`, `************1111`, `XXX.XXX.1234`. Static masking functions of this kind run when copying production data to test environments.

blocks.md:
**Dynamic data masking and its limit.** SQL Server's dynamic data masking applies a mask function to a column (`default()`, `email()`, `random()`, `partial()`) for users without the `UNMASK` permission; administrators with `CONTROL` always see real values. Microsoft's own documentation is blunt about what it is for: it "doesn't aim to prevent database users from connecting directly to the database and running exhaustive queries", and users with ad hoc query rights can infer real values. The documented example: with `Salary` masked, a user runs a query that *filters* on the real value even though it *displays* zeros:

`SELECT ID, Name, Salary FROM Employees WHERE Salary > 99999 and Salary < 100001;`

The rows that come back reveal everyone whose salary is exactly 100,000. Repeat with other ranges and the column is recovered. Microsoft's advice: use masking to prevent accidental exposure, and use auditing (lesson 9) wherever ad hoc access is granted.

Dynamic masking changes what is displayed, not what can be queried. Against anyone who can write their own WHERE clauses it is not a security boundary; use column permissions (lesson 8), tokens or encryption there.

blocks.question: An attacker steals the full orders database of a shop that uses vault tokenisation. What do they get for card numbers?
options: The card numbers, because the token is an encoding of them
Random tokens that only the vault can map back to card numbers
Card numbers, but only the last four digits
Encrypted card numbers they can brute-force offline
blocks.explain: Vault tokens are random and the mapping lives only in the vault, so there is nothing to decode or brute-force in the stolen table. Vaultless tokens (FPE, AES-SIV) are different: anyone with the key can reverse them.

blocks.question: Why is FPE a poor fit for tokenising 4-digit PINs?
options: With only 10,000 possible inputs the domain is far below NIST's proposed one-million minimum, where attacks on FPE work
FPE cannot handle digits
The output would be longer than 4 digits
FPE is one-way, so PINs could never be recovered
blocks.explain: FPE preserves the alphabet and length, so it handles digits fine and keeps 4 digits. The problem is domain size: known attacks exploit small domains, and NIST's draft revision requires at least one million possible values. FPE is reversible with the key.

lessons.title: Database security I: accounts, grants, views and the revoke trap

blocks.md:
Most data theft from databases does not break the database. It uses an account that was allowed to read too much. So the first database control is boring and decisive: **separate accounts, each with the least it needs**.

Tiny example: one web app, one analyst, one migration tool. If all three share a single superuser login, then a SQL injection in the app (*Injection: when data becomes code*) can drop tables and read every column, the analyst's laptop holds a credential that can do the same, and the audit log cannot tell who did what.

**A role layout that holds up:**

- **Owner/migration role**: owns the tables and runs schema changes from the deployment pipeline. No human uses it day to day; the application never connects with it.
- **Application role**: exactly the statements the app issues, on exactly its tables. Often `SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE` and no `DELETE` (use a soft-delete flag), and never DDL (statements like `CREATE` and `DROP`).
- **Analyst role**: read-only, on views or on specific columns, never on raw restricted columns.
- **Break-glass admin**: a separate, monitored account for emergencies.

Passwords come from a secret store at runtime (the Cloud security course), the database is not reachable from the internet (private endpoints, the same course), and row-level security keeps tenants apart (lesson *Multi-tenant isolation: tenant ids everywhere, row-level security* in *Broken access control and authorization design*).

blocks.caption: PostgreSQL 17. Run as the owner. `REVOKE ALL ... FROM PUBLIC` is belt and braces (PostgreSQL grants nothing on tables to PUBLIC by default) and removes any grant added later by mistake; the analyst gets three columns plus a masked view.
Real output from PostgreSQL 17, trimmed to the lines that matter.

blocks.md:
**Why the view works.** In PostgreSQL, by default "access to the underlying base relations referenced in the view is determined by the permissions of the view owner". The analyst has no right to the `ssn` column, but the view's owner does, and the view only ever returns the last four digits. That makes views a clean way to publish a reduced, masked shape of a table. If you want the opposite, a view that checks the *caller's* rights, current PostgreSQL versions offer the `security_invoker` option.

Unlike SQL Server's dynamic masking in lesson 7, the analyst cannot filter on the real `ssn`: the view never exposes it, and the base table refuses them.

blocks.prompt: A DBA wants an intern to read everything in `customers` except `ssn`. They run `GRANT SELECT ON customers TO intern;` then `REVOKE SELECT (ssn) ON customers FROM intern;`. What happens when the intern selects `ssn`?
blocks.reveal:
The intern **can still read it**. Real run on PostgreSQL 17:

```
SET ROLE intern;
SELECT name, ssn FROM customers WHERE id = 1;
   name   |     ssn
----------+-------------
 Ana Ruiz | 123-45-6789
```

PostgreSQL's GRANT documentation explains: a user may access a column if they hold the privilege for that column *or the whole table*, and "granting the privilege at the table level and then revoking it for one column will not do what one might wish". Grant the allowed columns explicitly instead.

blocks.title: Three roles, three different views of one table

scenes.caption: The owner role owns the table and runs migrations from the pipeline. Nobody connects with it at runtime.
The app role can SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE on the table, but not DELETE or change the schema. A SQL injection in the app inherits only these rights.
The analyst reads three plain columns directly and the rest only through the masked view, which runs with its owner's rights and returns the last four SSN digits.
The trap: a table-level grant plus a column-level revoke. The table grant still covers ssn, so the intern reads every column.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** Review grants as code: keep the `GRANT` statements in the repository and alert when the live database differs. Query the catalog for risky grants regularly: roles with table-level `SELECT` on tables holding restricted columns, roles that can log in and own objects, and any grant to `PUBLIC`. Rotate the application password through the secret store, and make sure each human and service has its own login, so lesson 9's audit log can name who did what.

Separate owner, application, analyst and admin roles; grant explicit columns or views rather than whole tables; never rely on revoking one column from a table-level grant; and keep grants in version control so drift is visible.

blocks.question: The app connects with a role that has SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE on `orders` but no DELETE and no DDL. An attacker finds SQL injection in the app. What do these grants limit?
options: Nothing: injection bypasses database permissions
The attacker can read only the masked view
The attacker can still read and change orders through the app's rights, but cannot delete rows or drop tables
Injection is impossible because of the grants
blocks.explain: Injected SQL runs with the application's database role, so it gets exactly the app's rights: still serious (read and modify), but no DELETE or DROP. Grants limit damage; parameterised queries prevent the injection itself.

blocks.question: How should a DBA let a role read every column of `customers` except `ssn` in PostgreSQL?
options: GRANT SELECT on the table, then REVOKE SELECT (ssn)
GRANT SELECT on the table and tell users not to query ssn
Rename the ssn column
GRANT SELECT (id, name, email, created_at) on the table, listing only the allowed columns
blocks.explain: A table-level grant covers every column, and a column-level revoke does not subtract from it, as PostgreSQL's documentation warns and the demo shows. List the allowed columns, or publish a view.

lessons.title: Database security II: auditing reads and the Snowflake thefts

blocks.md:
Grants say what an account *may* do. An audit log says what it *did*. When data is stolen through a valid login, the audit log is often the only place the theft is visible: the account was allowed to read the table; it just had never read four million rows at 3 a.m. before.

Tiny example: an analyst account normally runs 20 queries a day that return a few hundred rows. Today the same account lists every table, then exports the largest one. No permission was violated. Only a record of reads, compared with what is normal for that account, shows something is wrong.

**What PostgreSQL offers.** The built-in setting `log_statement = all` writes every statement to the server log. pgAudit, an open-source PostgreSQL extension, explains why that is not enough for an audit: the standard log "shows what the user requested, while pgAudit focuses on the details of what happened while the database was satisfying the request". Its **session** audit logging takes classes of statements: `READ` (SELECT and COPY from a table), `WRITE`, `FUNCTION`, `ROLE` (GRANT, REVOKE, role changes), `DDL`, `MISC`. Its **object** audit logging uses the permission system to pick exactly which tables or **columns** to log: grant the audit role `SELECT` on one column, and only statements that read that column are logged.

Each entry is a comma-separated record: audit type, statement and sub-statement ids, class, command, object type, object name, the statement and (optionally) its parameters. pgAudit's own caveat: audit logging is "best-effort and not transactional", so ship logs off the server quickly and alert if they stop.

blocks.code:
# postgresql.conf (session logging of reads, writes, role changes, DDL)
shared_preload_libraries = 'pgaudit'
pgaudit.log = 'read, write, role, ddl'
pgaudit.log_relation = on      # one entry per table touched
log_line_prefix = '%m %u %d [%p]: '   # time, user, database, pid

-- SQL, as a superuser: object logging of every read of customers.ssn
CREATE EXTENSION pgaudit;
CREATE ROLE auditor NOLOGIN;
-- and in postgresql.conf: pgaudit.role = 'auditor'
GRANT SELECT (ssn) ON customers TO auditor;

-- shape of an entry, from pgAudit's documentation:
-- AUDIT: SESSION,2,1,READ,SELECT,,,select *
blocks.caption: Configuration following pgAudit's README (not run here). The auditor role never logs in; its grants only select what gets audited. Column-level grants to it mean queries that never touch ssn produce no object-audit entries.

blocks.md:
**Case: Snowflake customer thefts, 2024, from the database side.** *Cloud security and IAM* covered why this happened: credentials stolen by infostealer malware, some from as far back as 2020, no MFA and no network allow lists. Here is what the intruders did once logged in, as Mandiant (Google's incident response firm) documented for the group it tracks as UNC5537, with about 165 potentially exposed organisations notified:

1. `SHOW TABLES` to list every database and table.
2. `SELECT * FROM` tables of interest.
3. `CREATE TEMPORARY STAGE`: a **stage** in Snowflake is a named location for files being loaded or unloaded; a temporary one is deleted when the session ends.
4. `COPY INTO @stage FROM (SELECT * ...)` with GZIP compression, to unload whole tables into files.
5. `GET @stage file:///...` to download the files.

Nothing here is an exploit. Every step is a normal command a data engineer might run, which is exactly why detection must look at the *sequence* and the *account*.

blocks.title: One theft session, as the query log records it

scenes.caption: Illustrative session built from the command sequence Mandiant published; times are invented. Login comes from a VPN address the account has never used.
Reconnaissance: SHOW TABLES across databases, and a few SELECTs to look at contents. Each line lands in query history.
Staging: a temporary stage is created and whole tables are unloaded into it as compressed files with COPY INTO.
Download: GET pulls the files out. When the session ends the temporary stage disappears, but the query history keeps every statement.

Where controls cut in: MFA or a network policy stops the login; PREVENT_UNLOAD_TO_INTERNAL_STAGES blocks this COPY (rows can still be read with SELECT, so it slows theft, not stops it); a sequence rule on query history raises an alert.

blocks.caption: Python 3, run as shown. Output: `902 j.doe [0, 1, 2, 3] ALERT: stage-and-download pattern`. Sessions 901 and 903 match no step and print nothing: the ETL (extract, transform, load) job's COPY loads into a table (COPY INTO sales), it does not unload to a stage.

blocks.md:
**Controls in Snowflake terms.** A **network policy** has an allowed list and a blocked list of network rules, and blocks always win. The account or user parameter `PREVENT_UNLOAD_TO_INTERNAL_STAGES`, when TRUE, prevents "unloading data from Snowflake tables to any internal stage, including user stages, table stages, or named internal stages"; it defaults to FALSE ([parameter reference](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/parameters)). For detection, the `ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY` view keeps 365 days of queries with their text, but Snowflake notes its latency "may be up to 45 minutes", so near-real-time alerting needs another feed.

**Database activity monitoring** (DAM) is the general name for tools that collect database audit records or traffic and alert on them, the database equivalent of the log pipelines you met in the cloud course. Whatever you use, the questions are the same: which accounts read restricted columns, how many rows, from where, and does that match their history?

Log reads of restricted data, not just changes: pgAudit object logging on sensitive columns, warehouse query history, cloud data events. Alert on sequences (list everything, stage, export, download) and on volume compared with the same account's normal.

blocks.question: Why could a rule that alerts only on failed logins and permission errors miss the Snowflake thefts entirely?
options: The intruders used valid credentials and ran commands their accounts were allowed to run, so nothing failed
Snowflake does not log failed logins
The intruders deleted the audit logs
Temporary stages hide queries from the query history
blocks.explain: Every step used a valid password and permitted commands, so there were no failures to alert on. The query history still recorded each statement; the temporary stage disappears at session end, but the COPY and GET statements remain in history.

blocks.question: In pgAudit, how do you log only the statements that read `customers.ssn`?
options: Set pgaudit.log = 'all'
Set pgaudit.role to an audit role and GRANT SELECT (ssn) ON customers to that role
Set log_statement = 'all'
Revoke SELECT on ssn from everyone
blocks.explain: Object audit logging uses the audit role's permissions as a selector: a column grant to the auditor means statements touching that column are logged. Session logging with 'all' or log_statement logs everything, which is noisier and harder to search.

blocks.md:
**DLP** (data loss prevention) is the family of tools and policies that recognise sensitive data and stop or flag it when it moves somewhere it should not: an email to an outside address, a USB stick, a personal cloud drive, a public share. "Loss" here means losing control of the data, not deleting it. Microsoft describes Purview DLP as monitoring and protecting against "oversharing", and says it covers data at rest, in use and in motion across email, file storage, chat, devices and more.

Every DLP decision has two halves: **is this content sensitive?** (this lesson) and **is this action allowed for this person, here?** (lesson 11). The first half reuses everything from lessons 2 and 3.

**Four ways to recognise content:**

- **Labels**: if a document carries a sensitivity label (lesson 3), the rule can act on the label without reading the content.
- **Patterns with checksums and context**: the sensitive information types of lesson 2. Broad: they find *any* card number, including ones that are not yours.
- **Exact data match (EDM)**: matching against *your* actual records. In Purview, you upload a table of real values (Microsoft says it can hold up to 100 million rows and be refreshed daily), but only as salted one-way hashes, "so your sensitive data is never in the open". A **primary element**, such as an SSN, must first be found by a pattern; EDM then checks its hash against the table and looks for **secondary elements** (name, date of birth) from the same row nearby. The aim, in Microsoft's words, is to "result in fewer false positives".
- **Fingerprints and trained classifiers**: matching documents derived from a known template, or machine-learning models trained on examples of a category such as contracts.

blocks.caption: Python 3, run as shown. Output: `[('6789', 'EXACT: our customer, name nearby')]` then `[('3456', 'pattern only, not our customer')]`. A simplified model of EDM: only salted hashes of the customer table are needed at scan time.

blocks.md:
**The base-rate problem.** Suppose a mail gateway scans 200,000 outbound emails a day, and 1 in 1,000 (200 emails) really contains customer data going somewhere it should not. A detector that catches 95% of them (190) and wrongly flags just 1% of the clean ones flags about 1,998 clean emails. Of roughly 2,188 alerts, only 190 are real: a **precision** of about 9%. The analysts drown, users learn to click "override", and the policy gets switched to audit-only.

Because true leaks are rare, the false positive rate dominates. That is why EDM and context-based high confidence matter: cutting false positives from 1% to 0.1% lifts precision to about 49%, and to 0.01% lifts it to about 90%, with the same recall.

blocks.caption: p is the share of messages that truly contain a leak (prevalence), r the detector's recall, f its false positive rate. With p = 0.001, r = 0.95, f = 0.01: 0.00095 / (0.00095 + 0.00999) = 0.087.

blocks.title: Precision of a DLP rule as its false positive rate falls

scenes.caption: Prevalence 1 in 1,000 and recall 95%. At a 1% false positive rate (right side) fewer than 1 alert in 10 is real.
Same detector, but leaks are ten times rarer (1 in 10,000); the dots keep the 1 in 1,000 values. Precision collapses: rarer events need even lower false positive rates.
Back to 1 in 1,000. Moving from pattern matching (say 1%) to exact data match (say 0.01%; illustrative rates) is what takes a rule from noise to something analysts can act on.

blocks.prompt: Your card-number DLP rule fires on 40 emails a day, and almost all are internal test data containing the standard test card 4111 1111 1111 1111. What is the best fix?
blocks.reveal: Exclude known test numbers (Microsoft's built-in card type already does), and require **high confidence**, meaning a card number plus context such as an expiry date or a CVV keyword. Do *not* widen the rule into an allowlist for the whole test team's mailbox: that would also exempt a real leak from those mailboxes. Fix the detector's precision, not the scope.

blocks.md: DLP is only as good as its detector's precision. Prefer labels and exact data match over generic patterns where you can; require context for high confidence; and measure precision on real traffic before turning on blocking. Hashed SSNs are not anonymous: with about a billion possible values, anyone holding the salt can hash them all, so guard the EDM hash file and salt as Restricted data.

blocks.question: What does exact data match add over a pattern-based SSN detector?
options: It finds SSNs in images
It encrypts the SSN before sending
It confirms the number is one of your own records (via salted hashes) and can check for matching fields from the same row nearby
It removes the need for a pattern
blocks.explain: EDM compares hashes of found values against hashes of your table, and then looks for secondary fields from the same record, which cuts false positives sharply. It still needs a pattern-based type to find the primary element first.

blocks.question: A DLP rule has 95% recall and a 1% false positive rate. Real leaks are 1 in 1,000 messages. Roughly what share of its alerts are real?
options: About 9%
About 95%
About 50%
About 1%
blocks.explain: Per 200,000 messages: 190 true alerts and about 1,998 false ones, so 190 / 2,188 is about 8.7%. Recall is 95%, but precision is low because clean messages vastly outnumber leaks.

lessons.title: Where DLP acts: endpoints, email, web and cloud

blocks.md:
Recognising sensitive content is half the job. The other half is being **in the path** when someone tries to move it, and deciding what to do. DLP tools sit at four kinds of places, and each sees different things.

Tiny example: an employee wants a customer list at home. They could email it to a personal address, upload it to a personal cloud drive in the browser, copy it to a USB stick, print it, or paste it into a chat. Each route passes a different control point, or none.

**Network and web DLP** inspects traffic leaving the network through a proxy. Almost all of that traffic is HTTPS, and TLS hides content from anything in the middle (*How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender*). To inspect it, the proxy must perform what CISA's alert TA17-075A calls "a man-in-the-middle (MiTM) attack on the connection": it terminates TLS, inspects, and re-encrypts to the real server, which requires installing the proxy's certificate as trusted on every client. CISA warned in 2017 that many such products did not properly verify server certificates before re-encrypting, weakening the protection HTTPS gives, and advised organisations to weigh the trade-offs before deploying ([CISA TA17-075A](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2017/03/16/https-interception-weakens-tls-security)). Endpoint agents and managed browsers avoid that trade-off in a different way: they see the content on the device, before it is encrypted for the network.

blocks.title: One outbound email through DLP: tip, override, audit

scenes.caption: A user attaches a spreadsheet and addresses it to a personal Gmail account. The mail client checks the draft against policy.
The classifier finds 340 card numbers with expiry dates (high confidence). The policy for external recipients is 'block with override'.
The user sees a policy tip explaining why. They may cancel, or override with a business justification.
The user overrides with 'working from home'. The message goes, and the event, justification and file details go to the audit log.
An analyst reviews overrides daily. A single override is a conversation; a pattern of overrides by a departing employee is an insider risk signal (lesson 12).

blocks.md:
**Actions, from gentle to strict.** Microsoft lists the range: audit only; show a **policy tip** warning the user; **block with override**, capturing the user's justification; block without override; and for data at rest, quarantine. All DLP activity goes to the audit log by default.

**Roll out in simulation first.** Microsoft recommends deploying policies in **simulation mode**, where actions are not applied, measuring what would have happened, tuning, then moving to tips, then blocking. A blocking rule with poor precision (lesson 10) breaks real work and teaches people to route around it.

**What DLP cannot see.** Content it cannot read: files encrypted by the user, data typed by hand into a personal device, a phone camera pointed at the screen. Channels with no control point: an unmanaged laptop, a personal phone on mobile data. DLP is excellent at stopping mistakes and slowing casual leaks; against a determined insider it mainly creates evidence, which is why lesson 12 exists.

blocks.code:
# Toy policy engine: what happens when content meets a channel
POLICY = {   # (detector confidence, destination): action
    ("high", "external_email"): "block_with_override",
    ("high", "usb"):            "block",
    ("high", "personal_cloud"): "block",
    ("low",  "external_email"): "policy_tip",
    ("low",  "usb"):            "audit",
}

def decide(confidence: str, destination: str, simulation: bool) -> str:
    action = POLICY.get((confidence, destination), "allow")
    if simulation and action not in ("allow", "audit"):
        return "audit (simulation: would " + action + ")"
    return action

events = [("high", "external_email"), ("high", "usb"), ("low", "usb"), ("low", "intranet")]
for sim in (True, False):
    print("simulation" if sim else "enforced  ", [decide(c, d, sim) for c, d in events])
blocks.caption: Python 3, run as shown. Output: `simulation ['audit (simulation: would block_with_override)', 'audit (simulation: would block)', 'audit', 'allow']` then `enforced ['block_with_override', 'block', 'audit', 'allow']`. A toy model of how a policy maps confidence and destination to an action.

blocks.md: Every exception is a hole. Allowlisting a whole team, a whole domain or a whole application because one rule was noisy removes protection from every future leak through that path. Fix the detector, then make narrow, reviewed exceptions with an expiry date.

blocks.question: A company wants to stop customer data being uploaded to personal cloud drives. Its web proxy does not decrypt TLS. Where can it still enforce this?
options: Nowhere: TLS makes uploads invisible
At the destination cloud provider's servers
In the email gateway
In the endpoint DLP agent and managed browser, which see the file before it is encrypted for upload
blocks.explain: Without TLS interception the proxy cannot see content, but the endpoint agent sees the file and the upload attempt on the device itself, before TLS. That is the 'upload to restricted cloud service domain' activity in Microsoft's endpoint DLP.

blocks.question: Why deploy a new DLP blocking rule in simulation mode first?
options: Simulation mode is faster
Because blocking rules are illegal in some countries
To measure how often it would fire and on what, and tune precision, before it blocks legitimate work
Simulation mode encrypts the data
blocks.explain: Simulation applies no actions but records matches, so you can measure false positives on real traffic and fix the detector or scope. Turning blocking on first usually breaks business processes and drives users to unmonitored channels.

lessons.title: Insider risk: definitions, the Tesla files and running a programme

blocks.md:
*Security from zero* listed insiders among the people who attack. This lesson treats them as a data security problem: the person already has legitimate access, so most controls in this course are, by design, letting them through.

**CISA's definitions.** An **insider** is "any person who has or had authorized access to or knowledge of an organization's resources". **Insider threat** is "the threat that an insider will use their authorized access, intentionally or unintentionally, to do harm". CISA sorts insider threats into *unintentional* (negligent: knows the rules and ignores them; accidental: mistypes an email address and sends a document to a competitor) and *intentional* (malicious: for gain or revenge), plus **collusive** (insiders working with an outside actor) and **third-party** (contractors and vendors with access). Many programmes and tools say **insider risk** instead, to cover mistakes as well as malice; Microsoft's product, for example, is called Insider Risk Management.

**Case: Tesla, 2023.** In May 2023 the German newspaper Handelsblatt reported it had received the "Tesla Files": more than 23,000 internal documents, about 100 gigabytes, including employee personal data, customer bank details, production secrets and customer complaints. In a data breach notice to Maine's attorney general in August 2023, Tesla said an investigation found that two former employees had leaked the data, including names, addresses, phone numbers, employment records and Social Security numbers of 75,735 current and former employees. Tesla sued the two, which led to the seizure of their devices, and obtained court orders forbidding further use or sharing of the data, [as TechCrunch reported](https://techcrunch.com/2023/08/21/tesla-breach-employee-insider/).

The data left with people who had or had had access. No password was cracked and no vulnerability exploited. Detection and response here are about behaviour and evidence, not malware.

**Signals an insider risk programme combines.** No single event means much; sequences do.

- **Context from HR**: a resignation or termination date, a poor review. Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management's *Data theft by departing users* template uses resignation and termination dates from an HR connector (or Entra account deletion) for this reason.
- **Data activity**: unusual volume of downloads compared with the person's own history; access to repositories outside their role.
- **Exfiltration routes**: DLP events from lesson 11 (USB copies, uploads to personal cloud, overrides with weak justifications, emails to personal addresses).
- **Attempts to avoid controls**: disabling security tools, renaming or compressing many files.

The CERT Division of Carnegie Mellon's Software Engineering Institute publishes the *Common Sense Guide to Mitigating Insider Threats*; its seventh edition (2022) gives 22 best practices drawn from more than 3,000 insider cases, written for management, HR, legal, physical security, IT, information security, data owners and software engineers.

blocks.caption: Python 3, run as shown. Output: `u17 100 review` and `u42 20 no alert`. A toy score: real tools weight many indicators, but the structure (a triggering event, then activity measured against the person's own baseline) is the same.

blocks.title: Two users, the same events, different stories

scenes.caption: User u17 resigns on day 1 with a last day of 19 September. Until now nothing about their behaviour has changed. Scale is in days of September.
Day 3: u17 downloads 412 files from the battery engineering share, about 20 times their daily normal. Inside a notice period this is weighted heavily.
Day 4: 380 files go to a USB stick. Endpoint DLP logs it. Combined with the resignation and the download spike, u17 scores 100 and goes to review.
User u42 reads 35 files from the same share (normal for their role) and copies two small files to USB a week later. One USB event alone scores 20: no alert.

blocks.md:
**Running it fairly.** Insider risk monitoring watches colleagues, so it needs rules of its own:

- **Proportion and law**: monitoring employees is regulated (in the EU, GDPR applies to employee data), so legal and HR sign off on what is collected and why, and staff are told that monitoring exists.
- **Privacy by design**: Purview, for example, pseudonymises users by default, so analysts see "user 17" until there is a reason to reveal a name, with role-based access and audit logs on the analysts themselves.
- **Response with HR and legal**: the outcome of a review is usually a conversation, retrieval of data, or access removal, coordinated with HR and legal, as in Tesla's case where lawsuits led to device seizure and court orders.
- **Prevention beats detection**: least privilege (lesson 8), fast removal of access on departure, and labels with DLP make the risky path harder in the first place.

Insiders already have access, so the programme rests on context (HR events, role), behaviour against the person's own baseline, and exfiltration routes, combined as sequences. Build it with HR, legal and privacy from the start, and pseudonymise until there is cause.

blocks.question: Under CISA's definitions, which of these is an insider threat?
options: An external attacker scanning the company's VPN
A contractor with valid access who mistakenly emails a customer file to the wrong external address
A phishing email arriving from outside
A public vulnerability report about the company's product
blocks.explain: An insider is anyone who has or had authorised access; the threat can be unintentional. A contractor is a third-party insider, and a misdirected email is CISA's own example of an accidental insider threat. The others are external events.

blocks.question: Why does an insider risk tool want an HR connector for departing users?
options: Because a resignation or termination date is the triggering context that makes download spikes and USB copies meaningful
To read employees' performance reviews in full
To revoke access automatically on the first day of employment
Because HR systems contain the DLP policies
blocks.explain: Departure is the context in which unusual data activity is most significant; Purview's 'Data theft by departing users' template takes that trigger from an HR connector (or from Entra account deletion). It does not need full reviews, and access removal is a separate identity process.

lessons.title: Media sanitisation: clear, purge and destroy (NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2)

blocks.md:
Every copy of data eventually sits on a physical device that will be reused, returned, sold or thrown away. **Media sanitisation** is making the data on it unrecoverable before that happens. The first surprise is that *deleting* does not do it.

Tiny example, run on a real machine: SQLite (a small database library embedded inside many applications) is told to `DELETE` a row holding an SSN. The database no longer returns it. Are the bytes still in the file?

blocks.code:
import os, sqlite3

def trial(path: str, secure: bool) -> bool:
    if os.path.exists(path):
        os.remove(path)
    db = sqlite3.connect(path)
    db.execute(f"PRAGMA secure_delete = {'ON' if secure else 'OFF'}")
    db.execute("CREATE TABLE t (ssn TEXT)")
    db.execute("INSERT INTO t VALUES ('123-45-6789')")
    db.commit()
    db.execute("DELETE FROM t")
    db.commit()
    db.close()
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        return b"123-45-6789" in f.read()      # is the 'deleted' value still on disk?

print("secure_delete OFF, bytes still in file:", trial("a.db", False))
print("secure_delete ON,  bytes still in file:", trial("b.db", True))
blocks.caption: Python 3 with SQLite 3.54, run as shown. Output: `secure_delete OFF, bytes still in file: True` then `secure_delete ON,  bytes still in file: False`.

blocks.md: **Why.** Deleting a row, like deleting a file, marks space as free and removes the pointer to it; the old bytes stay until something overwrites them. SQLite documents this: when `secure_delete` is on, "SQLite overwrites deleted content with zeros"; it is normally off for performance, and applications "that wish to avoid leaving forensic traces" should enable it or run `VACUUM`. Filesystems behave the same way, one layer down. And even overwriting may not reach the physical cells, as the rest of this lesson shows.

**NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2** (*Guidelines for Media Sanitization*, September 2025, replacing the 2014 Rev. 1) defines three methods:

- **Clear**: logical techniques over the normal interface (overwriting all user-addressable locations, or a factory reset where rewriting is not supported) that protect against "simple, non-invasive data recovery techniques". The device stays usable.
- **Purge**: physical or logical techniques that make recovery "infeasible using state-of-the-art laboratory techniques" while leaving the device potentially reusable: dedicated device sanitise commands (overwrite, block erase, cryptographic erase), or degaussing for magnetic media.
- **Destroy**: recovery infeasible with laboratory techniques *and* the device can no longer store data: disintegrate, incinerate, melt, pulverise, shred.

The standard says organisations should prefer purge to clear when possible, and choose based on the FIPS 199 confidentiality level of the data (lesson 3), whether the device will be reused, and whether it is leaving the organisation's control.

**What Rev. 2 changed.** It drops the old multi-pass overwrite habit: the 2025 text states that the clear method does not need multiple passes, countering "the obsolete DoD 5220.22-M language" (DoD 5220.22-M was a US Defense Department manual whose multi-pass overwrite patterns many wiping programs implemented; the Department removed overwriting specifications from it in 2006). Degaussing (erasing magnetic media with a strong reverse magnetic field) "should not be used for non-magnetic ISM (e.g., flash storage, such as SSDs)", and is not considered an approved destroy technique even when it leaves a drive inoperable. Device-specific techniques are delegated to IEEE 2883, a standard for sanitising storage from the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers). *ISM*, information storage media, is Rev. 2's new term, chosen to include cloud storage.

blocks.title: Why overwriting a file on an SSD can leave the old data

scenes.caption: Simplified flash translation layer (FTL). The OS sees logical blocks A to D. Block A, holding an SSN, is stored in physical flash page 0.
A wiping tool overwrites block A with zeros. Flash cannot be rewritten in place, so the FTL writes the zeros to a fresh page (4) and remaps A there.

The OS reads zeros and reports success. Page 0 is only marked stale: the SSN is still in the chips until garbage collection (the drive's own background clean-up of stale pages) erases it, which the user cannot control or verify.
Cryptographic erase: the drive always encrypted every page with an internal key. Sanitising the key leaves every page, stale ones included, as unreadable ciphertext.

blocks.md: **The evidence.** Michael Wei, Laura Grupp, Frederick Spada and Steven Swanson at UC San Diego tested this in 2011 by writing patterns to SSDs, sanitising them, then reading the flash chips directly ([*Reliably Erasing Data From Flash-Based Solid State Drives*](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/fast11/tech/full_papers/Wei.pdf), USENIX FAST 2011, the File and Storage Technologies conference). Their conclusions: built-in sanitise commands are effective, "but manufacturers sometimes implement them incorrectly" (on some drives the command reported success while all data remained); overwriting the entire visible address space twice is "usually, but not always" sufficient; and none of the tested single-file overwrite techniques worked: between 4% and 75% of a file's contents remained. Degaussing individual flash chips left the data intact in every case.

**Cryptographic erase (CE).** If everything on a device was always encrypted, destroying the key is enough. Rev. 2 calls CE a purge technique, notable because it is fast, and for cloud storage, where you never touch the physical disks, "CE may be the only viable purge sanitization technique option". Its conditions:

- No sensitive data was ever stored on the device in plaintext (CE only sanitises what was encrypted).
- Every copy of the key can be destroyed; CE is not trustworthy if keys were backed up or escrowed somewhere you cannot reach.
- Strong, validated cryptography (at least 128-bit security; ECB mode not allowed).
- Long-lived secrets: if future cryptanalysis or quantum computing could recover keys, CE "may not be an acceptable sanitization technique". Where the keys are wrapped with public-key algorithms, note that [NIST IR 8547](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/ir/8547/final) (October 2026) plans the move off quantum-vulnerable RSA and elliptic-curve schemes (deprecated after 2030, disallowed after 2035).
This is also how you make backups and old copies (lesson 4) unreadable at once: encrypt each dataset under its own key, and destroy the key when the data's retention ends.

On SSDs and flash, never trust file shredders or multi-pass overwrites. Use the drive's sanitise command or cryptographic erase (and verify the result), or physically destroy it. In the cloud, crypto erase of keys you control is usually the only purge you can perform.

blocks.question: A laptop SSD was encrypted with full disk encryption from the day it was issued. Under SP 800-88 Rev. 2, what is a fast purge option before reissuing it?
options: Run a single-file shredder on sensitive folders
Degauss the drive
Delete the user profile
Cryptographic erase: sanitise the encryption key, provided no copy of it survives elsewhere
blocks.explain: Because nothing was ever stored in plaintext, sanitising every copy of the key purges the data. Shredders fail on SSDs (Wei et al.), degaussing does not work on flash, and deleting a profile only removes pointers.

blocks.question: Why did single-file overwrite tools fail on SSDs in the 2011 UCSD study?
options: SSDs refuse write commands
The flash translation layer writes new data to fresh pages and leaves old pages holding the original until garbage collection
The tools used the wrong patterns
SSDs encrypt everything automatically
blocks.explain: Flash cannot be rewritten in place, so 'overwriting' a logical block writes elsewhere and remaps it; the old physical page keeps the data. Between 4% and 75% of file contents remained. Patterns do not matter when the write never reaches the old cells.

lessons.title: Disposal as a process: Morgan Stanley's drives and the certificate

blocks.md:
Sanitisation techniques fail less often than sanitisation *programmes*. Devices go to vendors, vendors use subcontractors, paperwork says "destroyed", and nobody checks that each serial number that left the building has a matching record of what happened to it.

**Case: Morgan Stanley, 2016 to 2022.** In 2016 Morgan Stanley decommissioned two Wealth Management data centres and hired a moving and storage company, which, the SEC (US Securities and Exchange Commission) said, "had no experience with, or expertise in, providing such data destruction services", to remove and wipe thousands of devices. According to the SEC's order, the moving company stopped using its e-waste partner and sold about 4,900 IT assets, including unwiped hard drives, to another firm, which resold them; some ended up on an internet auction site. In October 2017 an IT consultant in Oklahoma who had bought some of the drives emailed the bank to say they could access its data.

**The paperwork failure.** The contract required certificates of destruction. Instead, the buyer issued *certificates of indemnification*, which only said it had taken possession and the risk of loss. The moving company forwarded them calling them certificates of destruction, and the SEC found the bank did not review them; had it done so, it would have seen an unvetted sub-vendor and that the drives were not being wiped. The moving company also invoiced for wiping and degaussing that was never done.

**A second failure, in encryption.** Servers decommissioned from local branch offices were missing, 42 of them potentially holding unencrypted customer data. The devices had encryption capability, but it was not activated until 2018, and then, because of a manufacturer flaw, encrypted only newly written data. That is exactly the precondition for cryptographic erase from lesson 13: data written in plaintext before encryption is turned on stays plaintext.

**Outcome.** In July 2020 the bank notified about 15 million customers. The OCC (Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, a US bank regulator) assessed a USD 60 million penalty on 8 October 2020 for failures including vendor oversight and keeping an "appropriate inventory of customer data stored on the decommissioned hardware devices". The SEC added USD 35 million on 20 September 2022.

blocks.title: Where the chain of custody broke

scenes.caption: Morgan Stanley hands thousands of devices to the moving company, under a contract that requires wiping and certificates of destruction.
At first the mover works with an e-waste firm that wipes or destroys drives and issues real certificates of destruction.
Then the mover switches to selling unwiped drives to another firm. That firm issues certificates of indemnification, which say nothing about wiping.
The mover forwards them labelled as certificates of destruction, and invoices for wiping. Nobody at the bank reads them.
Drives are resold online. A buyer finds the bank's data and emails the bank in October 2017, which prompts the bank's investigation.

blocks.md:
**What a programme needs** (SP 800-88 Rev. 2 and the case together):

- **Inventory of data-bearing assets** by serial number, with the classification of the data each held. You cannot reconcile what you never listed.
- **A decision per asset**: reuse inside, reuse outside, return, or dispose; Rev. 2 treats devices that will not come back (warranty exchanges, resale, recycling) as leaving organisational control, and the choice of method must account for that.
- **Vendor oversight**: vetted vendors, no unapproved subcontractors, on-site sanitisation or tracked transport for high-sensitivity media.
- **A certificate per device**. Rev. 2 lists what it should record: manufacturer, model, serial number, media type and source, method (clear, purge, destroy), technique (for example crypto erase or degauss), tool and version, verification method, and the people who performed the verification and validation.
- **Reconciliation**: every serial number that left must match a certificate, and a missing or unsigned one is a potential breach to investigate.

blocks.code:
import csv, io

inventory = io.StringIO("""serial,asset,holds_customer_data
ZA1K9,db-01 disk 1,yes
ZA1L2,db-01 disk 2,yes
ZA7Q4,file-02 disk 1,yes
TP-0091,backup tape 91,yes
SW-33,core switch,no
""")
certificates = io.StringIO("""serial,method,technique,verified_by
ZA1K9,purge,crypto erase,R. Diaz
ZA1L2,purge,crypto erase,R. Diaz
TP-0091,destroy,incinerate,
""")

certs = {row["serial"]: row for row in csv.DictReader(certificates)}
for row in csv.DictReader(inventory):
    if row["holds_customer_data"] != "yes":
        continue
    c = certs.get(row["serial"])
    if c is None:
        print(f"MISSING  {row['serial']:8} {row['asset']}: no certificate, treat as lost")
    elif not c["verified_by"]:
        print(f"UNVERIFIED {row['serial']:6} {row['asset']}: {c['method']} claimed, nobody verified")
blocks.caption: Python 3, run as shown. Output: `MISSING  ZA7Q4    file-02 disk 1: no certificate, treat as lost` and `UNVERIFIED TP-0091 backup tape 91: destroy claimed, nobody verified`. The switch has no customer data and is skipped.

blocks.md: Disposal is a chain of custody: inventory by serial number, sanitise to the data's classification, use vetted vendors, require a per-device certificate naming method, tool and verifier, and reconcile every serial. Read the certificates.

blocks.question: A vendor returns a PDF titled 'Certificate of Destruction' listing a batch number but no serial numbers or method. What should the asset owner do?
options: Accept it: the title says destruction
File it and close the ticket
Reject it until it lists each device's serial number, the sanitisation method and technique, and who verified it, then reconcile against the inventory
Ask the vendor to add a company logo
blocks.explain: A certificate is only evidence if it can be matched device by device to the inventory and says what was done and by whom (SP 800-88 Rev. 2's list). In Morgan Stanley's case, documents that were not certificates of destruction at all went unreviewed.

blocks.question: Branch servers had disk encryption switched on years after deployment, and the product encrypted only newly written data. Why does a later cryptographic erase not sanitise them?
options: The data written before encryption was enabled is still plaintext on the disks, and destroying the key does nothing to it
Crypto erase never works on servers
The keys were too short
Crypto erase needs internet access
blocks.explain: Cryptographic erase only removes access to what was encrypted. SP 800-88 Rev. 2 makes 'no sensitive data previously stored in plaintext' a precondition, and the SEC order describes exactly this flaw.

lessons.title: Putting it together: a data security programme, and practice

blocks.md:
Each lesson closed one gap from lesson 1's picture of copies. A programme runs all of them continuously, for every dataset, with owners and measurements. Here is the loop, with the question each stage answers and the case that showed what happens without it:

- **Find** (lesson 2): where is it? *Pegasus*: one bucket mixed crew data, source code and secrets and was open to the internet until outsiders found it.
- **Label** (3): how bad is disclosure? Classification by damage, high-water mark, labels tools can read.
- **Keep less** (4): do we need it? *Tea*: ID photos promised to be deleted were still there.
- **Protect** (5 to 8): who can cause decryption, see real values, run which SQL? *OPM*: encryption cannot stop valid logins.
- **Watch** (9 to 12): who read it, where is it going, does behaviour fit? *Snowflake* and *Tesla*: valid access, abnormal use.
- **Destroy** (13, 14): is it really gone from every device? *Morgan Stanley*: drives sold with data on them.

blocks.title: The data security loop, and where each control sits

scenes.caption: Discovery feeds the inventory; classification turns each inventory entry into a label and handling rules.
Labels drive minimisation (retention schedules) and protection (encryption layer, tokens, masks, grants) per class.
Monitoring uses the same labels and detectors: audit logs on restricted columns, DLP on outbound channels, insider risk combining both with HR context.
At end of retention or end of device life, data is destroyed by deletion jobs, crypto erase or physical destruction, with certificates.
Findings loop back: every DLP hit or audit alert in an unexpected place is a discovery result that updates the inventory.

blocks.md:
**Measures that tell you the programme works** (each should have an owner and a trend):

- Share of known data stores scanned by discovery in the last 30 days, and the number of restricted findings in unexpected places.
- Share of Restricted fields with field-level encryption or tokenisation; number of roles with table-level access to restricted columns.
- Retention jobs: records past their deletion date that still exist, per store, including backups.
- DLP: precision of each blocking rule on reviewed samples, override rate, and overrides per user.
- Insider risk: alerts reviewed within the agreed time; departures with access fully removed by the last day.
- Disposal: devices retired versus certificates received and reconciled; anything unmatched is open.

**Where to practise (legally).** Use only systems you own or have written permission to test.

- [PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Information disclosure](https://portswigger.net/web-security/information-disclosure) has free labs on data leaking through error messages, backups and debug pages.
- [OWASP Juice Shop](https://owasp.org/www-project-juice-shop/) is a deliberately insecure shop; its guide has a [Sensitive Data Exposure](https://pwning.owasp-juice.shop/companion-guide/latest/part2/sensitive-data-exposure.html) chapter of challenges. Run it locally and find what it leaks.
- [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/) (free challenges from Carnegie Mellon University's CyLab) and the free rooms on [TryHackMe](https://tryhackme.com/) and [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/) cover log analysis and investigations like lessons 9 and 12.
- Build your own: initialise a local PostgreSQL, recreate lesson 8's roles and the revoke trap, and write the lesson 14 reconciliation for your own home devices before you sell one.

Data security is a loop: find, label, keep less, protect, watch, destroy, with each finding feeding back into the inventory. Measure each stage, and judge controls by who can still cause the data to be read.

blocks.question: A company encrypts every database with TDE, runs DLP on email, and has never run discovery. Which lesson-1 gap remains widest?
options: Data in transit
The databases' backups
Side-effect copies (exports, tickets, shares, buckets) that nobody knows exist, so no control is applied to them
Outbound email
blocks.explain: TDE protects the known databases and their backups against stolen media, and email DLP covers one channel. Without discovery, copies elsewhere are unprotected and unmonitored: the Pegasus pattern.

blocks.question: Which pairing of case and missing control is right?
options: Tea 2025: no TLS on uploads
Snowflake 2024: no field-level encryption
OPM 2015: no data classification
Morgan Stanley: no per-device certificate review or serial reconciliation
blocks.explain: Morgan Stanley's failures were vendor oversight, unreviewed certificates and missing inventory. Tea's was retention not enforced; the Snowflake thefts used valid credentials without MFA or network allow lists; at OPM, officials said encryption would not have stopped attackers with valid credentials.
